desc:
You are given an array nums and a list of queries. Each query is [l, r, t] and asks: is there a value that occurs at least t times in the subarray nums[l..r] (both ends included)? Every query satisfies 2 * t > r - l + 1, so such a value, if it exists, is unique (it is a strict majority of the subarray).

Return an array with one answer per query: the value, or -1 if no value occurs at least t times.

For example, nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1] with queries [[0, 5, 4], [0, 3, 3], [2, 3, 2]] gives [1, -1, 2].
constraints: 0 ≤ l ≤ r < nums.length, and (r - l + 1) / 2 < t ≤ r - l + 1
hints: Counting inside every query range takes O(n) per query. The guarantee 2t > length means any answer is a strict majority of the range, which is a very strong property.

If a value is a strict majority of a range, the Boyer-Moore voting candidate of that range is that value. Voting results of two adjacent pieces can be merged, so they can be precomputed in a segment tree.

Store (candidate, surplus) in each segment tree node and merge two nodes: equal candidates add surplus, otherwise the larger surplus wins with the difference. Then verify the candidate of the query range with binary search on the sorted list of positions of that value.
editorial: Voting gives only a candidate: if a majority exists it is the candidate, but the candidate may be wrong when there is none. So the plan has two parts. First find the candidate of nums[l..r] in O(log n) using a segment tree whose nodes hold Boyer-Moore pairs (value, surplus); two pairs merge by adding surplus when the values match and otherwise keeping the pair with the larger surplus, reduced by the smaller one. The merge is associative enough for majority detection, because cancelling two different values never removes a strict majority.

Second, verify the candidate. For every value store the sorted list of its positions; the occurrences inside [l, r] equal bisect_right(pos, r) - bisect_left(pos, l). If that is at least t return the candidate, else -1. Total time is O((n + q) log n), space O(n). A randomised alternative samples a few random positions in the range and checks each with the same binary search.
